candidate_sources.title: Petal Blight of Camellia
candidate_sources.snippet: The fungus Ciborinia camelliae (formerly Sclerotinia camelliae) attacks only opened flower parts. Small brown spots appear on petals, enlarge and cover the whole petal, then the whole flower becomes brown. Hard brown-to-black sclerotia develop in the base of old infected flowers and later produce mushroom-like apothecia which release spores to cause new petal infections. Sclerotia can survive in soil at least 4 years.

candidate_sources.title: Camellia Petal Blight / Home and Landscape / UC Statewide IPM Program (UC IPM)
candidate_sources.snippet: Camellia petal blight, caused by Ciborinia camelliae, causes small brown spots on petals that enlarge until the whole flower becomes brown and mushy. A ring of white or gray mycelium can be seen at the base of the petals after removal of the calyx. Sanitation — removing and disposing of infected flowers and plant debris — is the most effective management strategy.

candidate_sources.title: Camellia-Flower and Petal Blight | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: Flower and petal blight of camellia is caused by Ciborinia camelliae. Infected petals develop prominent dark brown veins giving a netted appearance; flowers turn brown and collapse. Sclerotia form in the base of infected flowers and produce apothecia each year, surviving in soil 3 to 5 years. Management focuses on sanitation and removing infected flowers.
